Xactimate & Estimating.description: Plaster wall height at 8 foot 3 inches - extra 3 inches means more money on the estimate
Xactimate & Estimating.original_description: Don't leave money on the table. If you have plaster walls chances are your wall height is 8' 3". That extra 3" may not seem like a lot, but you can do the math in your head. 8' Ã 12" is 96". So a regular 8' wall is pretty close to 100". So that extra 3" is roughly 3%. Actually a tiny bit more than 3%. So let's say you have $10,000 worth of wall painting. 3% of that equals $300, before O&P and sales tax. So who is telling me that the price for an estimator should be a $350 flat fee? The 3" difference is almost equal to the low price estimator fee on just one measurement error on one line item.  Also, getting your measurements and your sketch correct gives a lot of credibility to the estimate. You can go round and round with subjective arguments all day long about whether something is high grade or low grade. But when you're negotiating with the insurance company or going to appraisal  and you can say that your measurements are accurate and the other person's measurements are not, that's not a subjective difference.

Claims Strategy & Insurance Law.description: Newest trend in claims adjusting - carriers taking money back from policyholders
Claims Strategy & Insurance Law.original_description:
I've been saying this forever. See this scene in a detective movie. They 1) revisit the crime scene, presumably to examine PHYSICAL EVIDENCE and 2) "chat up the neighbors", presumably to gather HUMAN INTELLIGENCE AKA EYEWITNESS TESTIMONY.

This is routine in investigations.

Unless it's an engineer doing an "investigation" for an insurance carrier. They do #1 but never #2.

They never ask anyone who witnessed the hail or the wind. They never ask the homeowner when repairs were done, before or after the wind event. They never ask when the shingles were last installed. They never ask about things that would corroborate the wind event like trash cans blowing down the street, trees falling over, and they don't ask about things that would corroborate hail like damaged vehicles. They just don't ever ask.

Why do detectives and police officers always do #1 and #2 but engineers only do #1?

Contractors & Bad Faith.description: How to tell that a General Contractor has been in business a long time
Contractors & Bad Faith.original_description: Best way to attach a sole plate or so plate to the slab on a new pour is to use a j-bolt. On a retrofit the best way is to drill a hole and epoxy a bolt. In California the contractor will be babysat by a deputy inspector who watches the process and signs off on it. Because of earthquakes. The next best method is to use a redhead, one of these expansion bolts, they're supposed to go in 7 in but a lot of people use the shorter ones and as long as the building inspector doesn't see the Box they might get away with it because you can't tell from looking once it's installed. But you shouldn't do that and it's probably not code compliant as far as I know in California but it's okay in other states to use those expansion bolts. One brand name is redhead and people often refer to him by the brand name. The least effective method is the one I'm doing here just to hold my soleplate temporarily, it's a powder actuated nail gun that drives a nail into the concrete. It uses a little 22 caliber blank and you can choose from different loads. All of these things are in Xactimate.
